title: Diurnal glycogen metabolism drives rhythmic liver protein secretion
projectDescription: The liver secretes most circulating proteins, which are critical for inter-organ communication and systemic energy homeostasis. However, the regulatory mechanisms governing hepatic protein secretion are largely unknown. Using proteomics approaches in humans and mice, we here demonstrate that hepatic protein secretion follows a 24-hour rhythm which is modulated by the timing of food intake. Rhythmic variations in the expression of secretory pathway proteins, involved in protein glycosylation and folding in the endoplasmic reticulum and Golgi apparatus, mediate this process. We find that feeding rhythms and the circadian clock protein BMAL1 regulate diurnal hepatic protein secretion by driving glycogen breakdown which generates glycosylation substrates. Rhythmic secretion was attenuated in a mouse model of obesity and affected by genetic variants associated with glycogen storage disease and congenital disorders of glycosylation. Our study reveals a mechanistic link between glycogen-derived metabolites and protein secretion, thereby connecting nutrient intake with fundamental liver functions.
sampleProcessingProtocol: Mouse plasma protein samples were digested, and peptides purified using previously established methods 87. LC-MS/MS analysis of these samples used the scanning SWATH methodology on a Sciex 6600 mass spectrometer with a 5-minute gradient as described previously 113.
dataProcessingProtocol: Raw MS data were analyzed using quantitative DIA proteomics software DIA-NN (v. 1.8). The complete mouse proteome databased from Uniprot was used for neural network generation, with deep spectral prediction enabled. Protease digestion was set to trypsin allowing for 1 missed cleavage and one variable modification. Oxidation of Met and acetylation of the protein N-terminus were set as variable modifications. Carbamidomethyl on Cys was set as a fixed modification. Match between runs and remove likely interferences were enabled. Neural network classifier was set to double-pass mode. Protein interferences were based on genes. Quantification strategy was set to any liquid chromatography (LC, high accuracy). Library profiling was set to smart profiling.
